routes.label: Count how many files disks can hold

question: Jamal wants to store \(30\) computer files on floppy disks, each of which has a capacity of \(1.44\) megabytes (mb). Three of his files require \(0.8\) mb of memory each, \(12\) more require \(0.7\) mb each, and the remaining \(15\) require \(0.4\) mb each. No file can be split between floppy disks. What is the minimal number of floppy disks that will hold all the files?
solution:
Every file size is a multiple of \(0.1\) mb, so the total stored on any disk is also a multiple of \(0.1\) mb. A disk with capacity \(1.44\) mb can therefore hold at most \(1.4\) mb of these files.

The three \(0.8\)-mb files must occupy separate disks, since two would require \(1.6\) mb. A disk containing a \(0.8\)-mb file cannot also contain a \(0.7\)-mb file or two \(0.4\)-mb files. It holds at most \(0.8+0.4=1.2\) mb.

The files require a total of
\[
3(0.8)+12(0.7)+15(0.4)=16.8\text{ mb}.
\]
With twelve disks, the three disks containing the largest files and the nine other disks could hold at most
\[
3(1.2)+9(1.4)=16.2\text{ mb}.
\]
This is insufficient, and fewer disks would hold still less. At least thirteen disks are necessary.

Thirteen disks suffice with the following packing:

Three disks each hold one \(0.8\)-mb file and one \(0.4\)-mb file.

Six disks each hold two \(0.7\)-mb files.

Four disks each hold three \(0.4\)-mb files.

These groups use all three large files, all twelve medium files, and \(3+12=15\) small files. Each disk holds either \(1.2\) or \(1.4\) mb, within its capacity. Thus the minimum is \(3+6+4=\boxed{13}\) disks, choice B.

solutionMethods.explanation:
Call the \(0.8\)-mb and \(0.7\)-mb files the larger files. The three \(0.8\)-mb files need separate disks and cannot share a disk with a \(0.7\)-mb file, because \(0.8+0.7=1.5>1.44\). The twelve \(0.7\)-mb files need at least six additional disks, since no disk holds more than two of them. Thus at least nine distinct disks contain a larger file.

Any disk containing a larger file holds at most two files altogether: even a \(0.7\)-mb file with two smallest files would require
\[
0.7+0.4+0.4=1.5\text{ mb}.
\]
Every other disk holds at most three files, because four smallest files require \(1.6\) mb.

If there were at most twelve disks, choose nine that contain larger files. Those nine hold at most eighteen files, and the at most three remaining disks hold at most nine files. The total would be at most
\[
9(2)+3(3)=27
\]
files, fewer than the required thirty. Therefore at least thirteen disks are needed.

To achieve thirteen, use three disks for \(0.8+0.4\), six disks for \(0.7+0.7\), and four disks for \(0.4+0.4+0.4\), with sizes measured in mb. Each group fits within \(1.44\) mb, and the packing uses exactly the stated numbers of all three file sizes. Hence the minimum is \(\boxed{13}\) disks, choice B.
